issues.legal_issue: A raiyati interest does not automatically merge into a superior landlord interest when both interests come to be held by the same person, and it remains separate absent a clear intention to merge.
material_facts: The holder of the raiyati interest acquired the entire superior landlord interest in the land.
The land was part of a village community system in which preserving raiyati land served the interests of the community and its headman.
The holder sought to have the land recorded as being in the cultivating possession of the owner, but the evidence did not show that he intended thereby to end the raiyati interest.
Keeping the raiyati interest separate was beneficial to the holder, who retained rights as a raiyat in village lands.
issues.conclusion: The raiyati interest did not merge into the superior landlord interest and continued to exist separately.
issues.legal_principle: Apart from applicable statutory provisions, the union of superior and subordinate interests does not by itself cause merger; merger occurs only where an intention to merge is clear. In the absence of an express intention, courts consider the holder’s interest and duty in keeping the interests separate, as well as the holder’s conduct. The Court referred to the general doctrine reflected in Noomesh v. Rai Narain, Prosonna v. Jagat, Raja Kissen Dutt Ram v. Raja Mumtaz Ali Khan, Surja Narain Mandal v. Nand Lall Sinha, Ulfat Hossain v. Gayani Dass, Promotha Nath Roy v. Kishore Lal Sinha, Dakshavani Dasi v. Amrita Lal Ghosh, Lachanbati v. Bodhnath, and Re Fletcher. It noted that the special community features of the relevant land system could make the doctrine difficult to apply, but did not express a final opinion on its general application there.

rule.if: tenant_acquired_superior_interest and (community_duty_to_preserve_separate_interests or preserving_separate_interests_benefits_holder) and not clear_intent_to_merge

predicates.tenant_acquired_superior_interest: A person holding a subordinate land interest acquired the superior interest in the same land.
predicates.community_duty_to_preserve_separate_inte: The landholding system placed a duty on the holder to preserve the subordinate interest for the benefit of the village community.
predicates.preserving_separate_interests_benefits_h: The holder retained practical rights or benefits by keeping the subordinate interest separate from the superior interest.
predicates.clear_intent_to_merge: The holder expressly or by conduct clearly manifested an intention to end the subordinate interest by merging it into the superior interest.

issues.definition: When a subordinate and superior land interest come into one person’s hands, the subordinate interest continues separately if preserving it is required by community duty or benefits the holder and no clear intention to merge is shown.

issues.legal_issue: An entry describing land as being in the owner’s cultivation does not, by itself, negate a continuing raiyati interest or establish an intention to merge it into the superior interest.
material_facts: An earlier settlement record described the land as held by the holder as a raiyat.
After acquiring the superior interest, the holder sought an entry describing the land as being in the owner’s cultivation, and the settlement record was amended accordingly.
The entry described cultivation by the owner and did not state that the raiyati interest had ended.
The holder’s conduct and interests did not establish a choice to merge the two interests.
issues.conclusion: The later owner-cultivation entry was neutral as to the continuation of the raiyati interest, so it neither displaced the earlier raiyati status nor created a conflict requiring the later entry to prevail; the settlement decision did not bar the claim as res judicata.
issues.legal_principle: The meaning of a settlement entry must be assessed in context. An entry describing land as in the owner’s cultivation does not necessarily negate a raiyati interest. The Court distinguished Madan v. Kheelu, which did not hold that an owner-cultivation entry always negates raiyati rights, and explained that Sarda Devi v. Ram Louchan Bhagat concerned transfer of the landlord’s interest, not transfer of a co-existing raiyati interest. Because the entry did not decide that the raiyati interest had ceased, there was no need to challenge its correctness.

rule.if: land_title_dispute_with_settlement_entries and earlier_record_shows_subordinate_holding and later_entry_describes_owner_cultivation and not entry_expressly_ends_subordinate_interest

predicates.land_title_dispute_with_settlement_entri: A land-title dispute involves settlement records made at different times.
predicates.earlier_record_shows_subordinate_holding: An earlier settlement record describes the holder as holding the land under a superior interest.
predicates.later_entry_describes_owner_cultivation: A later settlement entry describes the land as being in the superior holder’s own cultivation.
predicates.entry_expressly_ends_subordinate_interes: The later entry expressly states that the subordinate interest has ended.

issues.definition: In a land-title dispute, a later entry describing owner cultivation does not negate the subordinate interest shown in an earlier record unless the later entry expressly ends that interest.

issues.legal_issue: Whether a subordinate land interest continued after the holder acquired the superior interest is a mixed question of law and fact when its resolution depends on applying the doctrine of merger to the circumstances.
material_facts: The trial court and first appellate court concluded that the raiyati interest had ceased after the holder acquired the superior interest.
The issue depended on applying the doctrine of merger to the land system and the holder’s conduct and interests.
The matter came before the High Court in a second appeal.
issues.conclusion: The question was a mixed question of law and fact, and the High Court was entitled to examine it in the second appeal.
issues.legal_principle: A question is not a pure question of fact when its resolution depends on the correct appreciation and application of a legal doctrine to the circumstances. The Court applied that principle to the doctrine of merger and the continued existence of the subordinate interest; no earlier case was cited for this particular conclusion.

predicates.second_appeal: The challenged decision is before a higher court in a second appeal.
predicates.subordinate_interest_depends_on_applying: Deciding whether a subordinate land interest continued requires applying a legal doctrine to the circumstances and conduct shown by the evidence.

issues.definition: In a second appeal, a question about continuation of a subordinate land interest is reviewable as a mixed question of law and fact when deciding it requires applying a legal doctrine to the facts.

issues.legal_issue: The availability of an administrative remedy for an invalid transfer does not exclude a civil court’s jurisdiction to decide title and whether the transfer is valid.
material_facts: The claim was a civil suit seeking a declaration and possession of land.
The title dispute depended on whether a transfer of a raiyati interest, whose transferability had not been recorded, conveyed title.
The governing provision gave an administrative officer power to evict a transferee and restore or resettle the land, while also directing courts not to recognize a prohibited transfer as valid.
issues.conclusion: The civil court could decide whether the transfer contravened the restriction and was required to dispose of the title dispute on the basis that no title passed if it did.
issues.legal_principle: The administrative remedy allowing an officer to evict a transferee and restore or resettle land was not intended to be exhaustive. The direction that courts must not recognize a prohibited transfer as valid requires a civil court hearing a title dispute to determine whether the transfer contravened the restriction and, if so, to proceed on the basis that the transferee acquired no title. This follows from section 27(2) and (3) of Regulation III of 1872.

predicates.civil_title_dispute: A civil proceeding asks the court to determine rights to land or possession of it.
predicates.claim_relies_on_prohibited_transfer: A party relies on a transfer that is alleged to have contravened a restriction on transfer.
predicates.courts_are_required_not_to_recognize_tha: The governing rule directs courts not to recognize a transfer made in contravention of the restriction as valid.

issues.definition: A civil court may determine title and the validity of an alleged prohibited transfer when the proceeding concerns land rights and the governing rule requires courts not to recognize that transfer.

issues.legal_issue: A transfer of a raiyati interest is ineffective to convey that interest when transferability was not recorded, although a separately held right to receive rent may pass.
material_facts: The holder’s raiyati interest continued separately from the superior landlord interest.
The right to transfer the raiyati interest had not been recorded for the land.
The successors in interest purported to transfer the land, and the dispute concerned the interest conveyed by that transfer.
The transfer could convey the separately held right to receive rent.
issues.conclusion: The transfer did not convey the raiyati interest, but it passed the right to receive rent.
issues.legal_principle: Section 27(1) of Regulation III of 1872 makes a transfer of a raiyat’s right in a holding invalid unless the right to transfer has been recorded, and section 27(2) bars courts from recognizing a transfer made in contravention of that requirement. The restriction applies to the raiyati interest, not to a distinct landlord interest that may coexist in the same person. The Court discussed Sarda Devi v. Ram Louchan Bhagat in distinguishing a transfer of the landlord’s interest from a transfer of the raiyati interest.

predicates.transfer_of_subordinate_land_interest: A holder or successor purports to transfer a subordinate land interest.
predicates.subordinate_interest_continues: The subordinate interest remains distinct from any superior interest held by the transferor.
predicates.transferability_not_recorded: The right to transfer the subordinate interest has not been recorded as permitted.

issues.definition: A purported transfer does not convey a continuing subordinate land interest when the right to transfer that interest has not been recorded.
